summary: Extends the procedures for building multicast trees that cross from IP into MPLS regions, using mLDP in the MPLS part, to the case where the link between regions is a VRF table link. It is mainly aimed at uses where VRFs support multicast applications other than multicast VPN.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7246 shows how a multicast tree can cross between an IP network and an MPLS core when the link between them belongs to a virtual routing and forwarding table. The tree is built with PIM in the IP part and with mLDP in the MPLS part. This RFC carries the PIM source and group addresses inside the mLDP signalling, together with the route distinguisher that names the VRF, so the receiving router can find the right table.

questions: multicast across mpls and ip regions
how does multicast cross mpls and ip regions
what is a vrf in multicast
subtitle: How a multicast tree crosses between IP and MPLS regions when the link between them sits in a VRF table.

tldr.problem: A multicast tree that crosses an MPLS core has to be built with PIM on the IP side and with mLDP in the core. The existing conversion procedures assume the border routers have a global route to the source, which fails when the border link belongs to a VRF.
tldr.mechanism: The mLDP opaque value is extended to carry the source or rendezvous point address, the group address and the route distinguisher, so the receiving router can find the right VRF. Four new encodings cover IPv4 and IPv6 source-specific and bidirectional trees.
tldr.outcome: A provider can carry multicast across an mLDP core for VRF-isolated customers without the full multicast VPN machinery, with one PIM tree per multipoint path. RFC 7246 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7438.

today: RFC 7246 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7438. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
An IP multicast distribution tree often starts and ends in regions of the network that do not use labels, and crosses a region that does. It is useful to build the tree as a plain IP tree, convert it into an MPLS multipoint label switched path when it enters the labelled region, and convert it back to a plain IP tree when it leaves.

RFC 6826 gives the procedures for that conversion: PIM in the non-MPLS regions, mLDP in the MPLS region, with the routers at the boundary converting between them. A PIM tree is identified by a source address and a group address, or by a rendezvous point address and a group address for a bidirectional tree. An mLDP tree is identified by a root address and an opaque value.

The procedures in RFC 6826 assume that the boundary routers have routes to the source address or the rendezvous point in their global routing tables. This RFC extends the procedures to the case where the interfaces that connect the two regions belong to a virtual routing and forwarding (VRF) table, as defined in the BGP IP/MPLS VPN specification. The RFC is aimed at cases where VRFs carry multicast applications other than multicast VPN.
sections.plainLanguage: A multicast tree often has to cross a network that uses labels in the middle and plain IP at both ends. RFC 6826 explains how to convert the tree at the borders. This RFC handles the harder case where the border link sits in a VRF table, so the routers there have no global route to the source.

sections.title: Terms and Acronyms
sections.content:
In-band signaling means using the opaque value of an mLDP FEC element to encode the source and group pair that identifies an IP multicast tree. The ingress LSR is the source of a point-to-multipoint path, also called the root node. An IP multicast tree is identified by a source IP address, a group address, or both. mLDP is Multipoint LDP. An MP LSP is a multipoint path, either point-to-multipoint or multipoint-to-multipoint.

The RPA is the rendezvous point address, used as the root of the distribution tree for a range of multicast groups. The RD is the route distinguisher, an identifier that makes a route unique in the context of a VRF. The UMH is the upstream multicast hop, the upstream router that lies on the path to the source of the multicast flow. A VRF is a virtual routing and forwarding table.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC uses short names for its parts. In-band signaling means writing the multicast source and group into the mLDP signalling. The RPA is the address where a bidirectional tree is rooted. The RD is the number that makes a route unique inside a VRF. The UMH is the upstream router on the path to the source.

sections.title: Scope and Configuration
sections.content:
The scope is limited to multicast content distributed in the non-MPLS regions by PIM-created source-specific or bidirectional trees. Bidirectional trees are always mapped onto multipoint-to-multipoint paths, and source-specific trees are always mapped onto point-to-multipoint paths.

The procedures do not support non-bidirectional PIM any-source multicast groups, do not support multicast trees other than mLDP multipoint paths in the core, and do not aggregate several PIM trees onto one multipoint path. Where those features are needed, the procedures of RFC 6513 and RFC 6514 apply. The RFC points at the case the procedures fit: a service provider offers multicast content to customers and uses VRFs to isolate those customers, without wanting aggregation.

To use the procedures for a group address in a given set of VRFs, those VRFs must be configured with a range of multicast group addresses for which mLDP in-band signaling is enabled. The configuration is per VRF, and the procedures apply to those groups only. The configuration must be present in every PE router attached to sites with senders or receivers for those groups.
sections.plainLanguage: Only two kinds of PIM tree are covered: source-specific trees and bidirectional trees. Any-source groups and merging several PIM trees into one path are not covered. Each VRF must list the group addresses that use this method, and every router that touches those groups must have that list.

sections.title: Signalling the Tree Across the VRF Link
sections.content:
Suppose a PE router, PE1, receives a PIM Join(S,G) message over an interface that belongs to a VRF. Following Section 5.1 of RFC 6513, PE1 determines the upstream route distinguisher, the upstream PE, and the upstream multicast hop (UMH) for the source address S.

To carry the tree over a multipoint path, PE1 sends an mLDP Label Mapping message. It holds a point-to-multipoint FEC for a source-specific PIM tree, or a multipoint-to-multipoint FEC for a bidirectional tree. The FEC has a root and an opaque value.

If the UMH and the upstream PE share an IP address, the root of the FEC is the IP address of the upstream PE. The opaque value then carries S, G and the upstream route distinguisher, and the S value is replaced by the rendezvous point address when the group is bidirectional. If the UMH and the upstream PE differ, the procedures of Section 2 of RFC 6512 apply: the root becomes the UMH, and the opaque value holds another FEC whose root is the upstream PE and whose own opaque value holds S or the rendezvous point, G and the upstream route distinguisher.

PE1 sends the Label Mapping on its LDP session to the next hop on the path to the upstream PE. When a PE router receives an mLDP message with such a FEC, and that router is itself the root, it uses the route distinguisher in the opaque value to work out which VRF it belongs to, and then follows the procedure of Section 2 of RFC 6826 in that VRF.
sections.plainLanguage: When a router receives a PIM join for a group, it looks up the upstream router and the route distinguisher for the source. It then sends an mLDP label mapping message whose root is that upstream router and whose opaque value holds the source address, the group address and the route distinguisher. The router at the root reads the route distinguisher, finds the matching VRF, and converts the mLDP tree back into a PIM tree there.

sections.title: The Four Opaque Value Encodings
sections.content:
The RFC defines four encodings for the opaque value, one for each combination of address family and tree type. Each is a TLV with a type code and a length, followed by the fields listed below.

  • Transit VPNv4 Source TLV: type 250, length 16. It carries an IPv4 source address (4 octets), an IPv4 group address (4 octets) and the route distinguisher (8 octets). It is used for a source-specific tree with IPv4 addresses.
  • Transit VPNv6 Source TLV: type 251, length 40. It carries an IPv6 source address (16 octets), an IPv6 group address (16 octets) and the route distinguisher (8 octets).
  • Transit VPNv4 Bidir TLV: type 9, length 17. It carries a mask length (1 octet), the IPv4 rendezvous point address (4 octets), the IPv4 group address (4 octets) and the route distinguisher (8 octets).
  • Transit VPNv6 Bidir TLV: type 10, length 41. It carries a mask length (1 octet), the IPv6 rendezvous point address (16 octets), the IPv6 group address (16 octets) and the route distinguisher (8 octets).

The mask length is the number of contiguous one bits, left justified, used as a mask. In the two bidirectional encodings the rendezvous point is the address used as the root of the distribution tree for the encoded group.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four ways to write the opaque value, one per combination of address family and tree type. The two source-specific encodings hold the source address, the group address and the route distinguisher. The two bidirectional encodings hold a mask length, the rendezvous point address, the group address and the route distinguisher instead of the source address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The same security considerations apply as for the base LDP specification in RFC 5036 and the base mLDP specification in RFC 6388.

Operators MUST configure packet filters so that the mechanism does not tunnel non-global-scoped IPv6 multicast packets outside their intended scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC adds no new security problems beyond LDP and mLDP themselves. Operators must set packet filters so that IPv6 multicast packets with a non-global scope stay inside their scope.
